title: Custom Stream Framing: Reconstructing Fragmented & Coalesced Raw TCP Byte Streams
solutionExplanation:
### Solution Breakdown: Zero-Leak Stream Framing
1. **Binary Concatenation**: `<<OldBufferBin/binary, IncomingChunkBin/binary>>` stitches incoming network slices without intermediary string conversion.
2. **Recursive Splitting**: `binary:split(Buffer, <<"\r\n">>)` strips the CRLF delimiter and isolates the first complete line.
3. **Memory Unpinning via `binary:copy/1`**: Both the extracted line tokens and the remaining partial slice are copied into independent binaries, guaranteeing that long-lived process heaps never retain references to temporary 64 KB socket buffers.

mentalModelCheck.question: When splitting an accumulated binary stream on "\r\n", why is calling binary:copy/1 on the remaining buffer essential for long-lived processes?

options.label: In Erlang, binary:split/2 creates sub-binaries that retain a reference to the entire original buffer. If that buffer was a 64KB ProcBin, omitting binary:copy/1 prevents the 64KB off-heap chunk from being garbage collected.
options.explanation: Precisely! A sub-binary is only a 24-byte pointer to an off-heap ProcBin. Without binary:copy/1, keeping even 3 bytes of remainder pins the entire 64KB socket chunk in memory, causing massive memory leaks across thousands of connections.

options.label: binary:copy/1 reverses the endianness of the bytes to big-endian.
options.explanation: binary:copy/1 performs a deep byte copy; it has nothing to do with byte order.

options.label: The BEAM VM will crash if a binary is passed between processes without being copied.
options.explanation: The BEAM seamlessly passes binaries across processes; binary:copy/1 is purely a memory-retention optimization.
